title: Day 13 — The Accelerometer as an I2C Device

slides.title: The Accelerometer as an I2C Device
slides.subtitle: ENGS 28 · Day 13 — In-Class

slides.title: Where we are
items: On Day 10 we wrote a device driver for the seven-segment display, on the I2C bus.
You read about the LSM303AGR accelerometer, its breakout board, and its WHO_AM_I register.
Today we'll wire it, verify that we can talk to it, and watch the transactions themselves on the logic analyzer.
slides.presenterNote: 110 minutes today: 3 settling + 2 announcements, then Parts of 8 / 22 / 6 / 24 / 15 / 15 / 12 / 3. Checkpoints at minute 35 (end of Part 2) and minute 65 (end of Part 4). Kits out now — the display STAYS wired all week; say so before anybody starts dismantling.

items: Back to I2C — a second device on the bus

slides.title: Back to I2C — a second device on the bus
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 8 min: 3 the resurface, 3 the commit, 2 the reveal. Her slides 3–5. The whole Part is recall plus one committed question; if it runs long, the reveal discussion compresses to one sentence (the cut order's third item).

slides.title: Do I have to take the display down?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 3 min, committed in writing with a reason. Her slide 4's question, verbatim. Collect a show of hands both ways before the reveal.

slides.title: The display stays
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min. REVEAL — show after the commit. Lab 7 grades exactly this (both devices, one bus), so land the address mechanism, not just the verdict.

slides.title: Wire it and verify the link
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 22 min — 3 the STEMMA slide, 15 the activity, 2 the whole-bus picture, plus 2 of checkpoint float — the day's tooling bottleneck (download, project copy, first build, four wires). Checkpoint at minute 35: if the room is not mostly printing, split hardware from software — re-seat the four wires against the photo; a failed build gets the verified-good file. A second re-seat failure gets immediate priority triage, not a wait for the checkpoint. Early finishers start Part 4's analyzer wiring now (DIO0/DIO1/ground) — it does not depend on Part 3.

slides.title: Four wires with a STEMMA QT Connector
Wire it, build it, verify the link
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 15 min: 10 for the project copy, download and first build, 5 for CoolTerm — the crucial step's first half: every board prints "Accelerometer initialized!" over its own wiring. Page back to the wiring slide while the room works.

slides.title: The whole bus: the display stays
What just ran
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 6 min: 4 the walk, 2 what 0x33 verifies. Her slides 10–11. The shift in (0x32 >> 1) is NOTICED here, not explained — Part 5 pays it off.

slides.title: lsm303_AccelRegisterRead() is one call into the I2C library
Put the analyzer on it
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 24 min: 3 the leads, 2 the Waveforms change, 4 the commit, 10 the capture, 2 the projected capture, 1 the close-up, 1 the reveal — plus 1 of checkpoint float. Checkpoint at minute 65: a student who cannot get a sweep marks the projected capture instead; the decoded values are the same by construction. A student whose WHOAMI never succeeded still captures, but only with the trick from later today — arm the single sweep, then press reset; a failing program stops after one transaction, so there is nothing repeating to trigger on.

slides.title: Wire the AD2's digital leads: DIO0 to SDA, DIO1 to SCL
Waveforms in logic mode: the decoder, and a wider time base
Predict: what will the decoder show?
Capture the WHO_AM_I read
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 10 min — the crucial step's second half: every student reads 0x19, 0x0F and 0x33 off their own decoded trace. The two #defines to compare against are at the top of whoami_test.c, open in each student's own IDE. The Waveforms setup screenshot is two slides back — page back for anyone whose screen doesn't match.

slides.title: What the decoder shows — and what predictions miss
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 1 min. REVEAL — show after the capture, against the projected trace. The two-transactions surprise is Part 5's opening; do not resolve it here.

slides.title: Digging deeper
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 15 min: 5 the questions (why-0x19 call-and-response first, then the two commits and their reveal), 4 the two kinds of NACK and the diagram in two halves (1+1), 6 the code walk in two halves. Her slides 24 / 29 / 12. Never cut the address-twice explanation or the two kinds of NACK — an unexplained double transaction, or an unexplained NACK inside a successful read, on their own screen is worse than not capturing at all. A student with a NACK-only trace works from the projected capture or a neighbor's for this Part.

slides.title: Why 0x19?
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 1 min, call-and-response — Day 9x's shift set-piece paying out; answer it aloud on the spot before the two committed questions.

slides.title: Digging deeper — against your own trace
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min, committed in writing: the address-twice question is confirm-on-your-own-trace (Day 10 said our memRead does stop-then-start), and who-ACKs is the day's subtlest question — there are FOUR acknowledge bits, one per byte.

slides.title: The answers, on the trace
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min. REVEAL — after the commits.

slides.title: The read transfers: the shape your trace has
Break it on purpose
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 15 min: 4 the commit, 7 the capture, 4 the debrief and stretch. Cut order inside this Part: the stretch tier first, then capture B becomes an instructor demo. Q3 IS OPEN: never assert from the front what the program prints on a wrong address — collect what the room saw instead.

slides.title: Break it: a wrong device address
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 8 min: 4 the predictions (in writing — most will predict a clean error message; this is the day's best wrong-guess moment), 4 the capture. Before anyone runs, say out loud: "If nothing happens on your screen, that is expected here — wait for the reset cue." Then the technique: single sweep armed, then reset, to catch the first transaction after startup.

slides.title: If you finish early: a wrong register address
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min to launch and debrief; fast finishers run it while the room debriefs. Second tier: the display's address question — a discoverable answer on their own desk.

slides.title: Stretch answers
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 1 min. REVEAL — after the capture-B trace is up. The 0x07 IS CTRL_REG1_A's power-on default — the DEFAULT column of the header, about to appear in Part 7, made visible on the wire.

slides.title: Accelerometer device driver
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 12 min: 2 the layers, 3 the recipe, 4 the header (2 the tour + 2 the download-and-check), 3 the prototypes. Boards reflash to 0x32 during the layers beat: launch the restore as the layers slide goes up and talk over it — layers and recipe are pure lecture and cost the room nothing. Then look up: is everyone back to 'Accelerometer initialized!'? That is the checkpoint for Parts 5–8. Not cuttable as a Part — Day 14 starts from it; if pressed, the recipe compresses and the header tour survives.

slides.title: Check the header against the datasheet
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min. Datasheet §7, Table 26 (p. 43) open on their laptops; the header goes into mylib, not Src.

slides.presenterNote: ≈ 3 min. End-of-class beats get cut by the clock unless protected — this one is the setup for Day 14's opening commit, so it is not the thing to cut.
